references.text: Parallel passage in Matthew's version of the same speech: Jesus says that two sparrows are sold for one small coin, and not one of them falls to the ground without the Father's will. Luke uses five sparrows for two coins, but the point is the same — God's care even for the smallest creatures, as an argument that the disciples need not fear ([ref:Matt 10:29-31|Matthew 10:29-31]).

The psalm praises God who gives food to the animals and to the young ravens that cry out. This shows God's care for all his creatures, including the birds — the same point Jesus makes when he says that not one sparrow is forgotten by God ([ref:Ps 147:9|Psalms 147:9]).

Jonah experiences that the Lord does not forget him, even in the depths of the sea. The phrasing "ἐπιλελησμένον ἐνώπιον τοῦ θεοῦ" (forgotten before God) in Luke reminds us that none of God's creatures are forgotten by him ([ref:Jonah 2:6|Jonah 2:6]).

The Lord assures that even if a mother could forget her child, he will never forget his people. Jesus' point that not one sparrow is "forgotten before God" reflects the same truth about God's unfailing care ([ref:Isa 49:15|Isaiah 49:15]).

The immediately following verse where Jesus draws the conclusion: You are worth more than many sparrows, and even the hairs on your head are numbered. The verse completes the argument that begins in verse 6 ([ref:Luke 12:7|Luke 12:7]).

Later in the same chapter, Jesus uses ravens as an example: They neither sow nor reap, yet God gives them food. Again, God's care for the birds is used as an argument to trust in God's care for people ([ref:Luke 12:24|Luke 12:24]).

God knows all the birds on the mountains. This psalm shows that God has oversight of and care for all living creatures, which supports Jesus' statement that no sparrow is forgotten before God ([ref:Ps 50:11|Psalms 50:11]).
